description.en: The backward jump is a plyometric exercise where you jump in reverse direction — pushing off and landing while moving backward. It trains backward jumping power, coordination, and proprioception. It is a less common but valuable plyometric variation, particularly for athletes who need rearward movement skills.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Arms at your sides. Make sure the area behind you is clear.
Sit your hips back into a partial squat. Swing your arms back to load the jump.
Explode upward and slightly backward by extending your hips, knees, and ankles.
Swing your arms forward to drive the backward momentum.
Land softly with bent knees, several inches behind your starting position.
Absorb the landing through your legs.
Immediately reset and prepare for the next backward jump.
Look slightly back periodically for safety. Aim for 5 to 8 reps per set.
Trains backward jumping power
Develops coordination and proprioception in less common direction
Useful for athletes with rearward movement needs
Builds explosive lower-body power
No equipment needed
Valuable plyometric variation

description.en: The band bench press is a chest pressing exercise performed lying on the floor with a resistance band looped under your back and gripped in both hands. It mimics the motion of a bench press without a bar or dumbbells. The band provides increasing tension at lockout, useful for at-home training.

en: Sit on the floor and loop a resistance band across your upper back, holding both ends.
Lie back on the floor. The band should be flat across your upper back beneath you.
Hold the ends of the band at chest height with palms facing forward.
Brace your core. Press both ends of the band straight up toward the ceiling.
Lock out at the top with arms fully extended. The band tension is highest here.
Lower under control back to your chest over two seconds.
Use a thicker band for more resistance, or step on more of the band for difficulty.
Perform 12 to 20 reps per set.
Effective at-home chest exercise
Increasing band tension loads the lockout
Highly portable
Easy to scale by changing band thickness
Joint-friendly with controlled loading
Useful when no bench or weights are available

description.en: The band bent over rear lateral raise is a strong rear delt isolation move using a band. The lifter steps on the band, bends over with a flat back, and raises the arms out to the sides. The bent angle hits the rear delts and rhomboids in their strongest position.

en: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet hip width.
Grip a handle in each hand with palms facing each other.
Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back.
Let the arms hang straight down with the band taut.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Raise both arms out to the sides until parallel to the floor.
Squeeze the rear delts and shoulder blades hard at the top.
Lower the arms back down with control.
Strong rear delt isolation
Builds upper back thickness
Easy to do anywhere
Useful posture builder
Strong band move
Trains the rhomboids

description.en: The resistance band single stiff leg deadlift with single arm row combines a single leg Romanian deadlift with a band row. The lifter hinges on one leg, rows the band at the bottom, and stands back up. It is a strong portable functional combo move.

en: Anchor a resistance band at floor level in front of you.
Stand on one leg with the opposite hand on the band handle.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Hinge at the hip and lift the back leg behind you.
Lower the torso toward parallel with the floor.
Row the handle up to the lower ribs at the bottom.
Lower the band and stand back up to the start.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Builds the posterior chain
Trains balance
Combines hinge and row
Strong portable combo
Useful functional move
Builds the back

description.en: The band squat twist combines a squat with a rotational core element using a resistance band anchored to the side. As you stand from the squat, you pull the band across your body, training rotational core strength and the legs together. The band provides constant resistance through the rotation.

en: Anchor a resistance band at chest height to a sturdy post.
Stand with the anchor on your right side, feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold the band with both hands extended to your right at chest height.
Step away from the anchor to create tension in the band.
Squat down by bending your knees and pushing your hips back.
As you stand back up, rotate your torso to the left and pull the band across your body.
Finish with the band pulled to your left hip and feet flat.
Reverse the motion back to the starting position. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Trains rotational core strength under load
Builds leg drive linked to core rotation
Constant band tension through the range
Strong carryover to athletic movement
Time-efficient compound combo
Easy to scale by changing band tension or step distance

description.en: The band upper crunch is performed lying on your back with a resistance band anchored low and gripped in both hands. As you crunch your shoulders off the floor, the band adds resistance to the contraction. It targets the upper rectus abdominis with the constant tension of bands.

en: Anchor a resistance band to a low point behind your head.
Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat.
Grip the band with both hands at your forehead.
Brace your core and engage your abs.
Crunch your shoulders off the floor by contracting your abs.
Allow the band to add tension to the contraction.
Squeeze your abs hard at the top of the crunch.
Slowly lower your shoulders back to the floor with control.
Adds band resistance to standard crunches
Constant tension through the range
Targets upper rectus abdominis
Allows progressive overload
Useful for home training
Easy to scale by changing band tension

description.en: The barbell decline bent arm pullover is performed lying on a decline bench while holding a barbell with bent arms. The bar is lowered behind the head for a deep stretch and pulled back over the chest. The decline angle increases lat stretch and the bent arms reduce shoulder strain.

en: Lie on a decline bench with feet hooked under the pads.
Hold a barbell over your chest with elbows bent.
Use a shoulder-width grip with palms facing forward.
Brace your core and keep your back against the bench.
Maintain the bent arm position throughout.
Lower the bar back behind your head in an arc.
Continue until you feel a deep lat and chest stretch.
Pull the bar back over your chest using the lats.
Deep lat stretch
Builds the lats and chest
Bent arms reduce shoulder strain
Decline angle increases stretch
Strong upper torso builder
Useful for chest and back

description.en: The barbell pin chest press is a bench press variation where the bar starts from pins set at chest level. Each rep begins from a complete dead stop, eliminating the stretch reflex and bounce. It builds raw concentric pressing strength right at the bottom of the bench press range.

en: Set safety pins in a power rack at chest level when lying on the bench.
Lie back on the bench with the loaded bar resting on the pins.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Plant your feet flat and pull your shoulder blades back.
Brace your core and engage your lats.
Drive the bar off the pins explosively, pressing through your chest and triceps.
Lock out at the top with arms fully extended.
Lower the bar back down to the pins with control. Reset before the next rep.
Builds dead-stop pressing strength
Eliminates the stretch reflex
Trains the bench press from its weakest position
Useful for breaking through bench press sticking points
Forces strict bracing and form
Strong carryover to competition bench press

description.en: The barbell reverse-grip bent over row (also called the Yates Row after Dorian Yates) is a horizontal pulling exercise performed with an underhand (supinated) grip. The underhand grip puts the biceps in a stronger pulling position and shifts emphasis to the lower lats and lower traps, building back thickness. The torso angle is typically more upright (about 60 to 70 degrees) than a standard bent over row.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart in front of a loaded barbell on the floor.
Hinge at the hips and grip the bar with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands roughly shoulder-width apart.
Stand up with the bar, then hinge forward at the hips until your torso is at roughly 60 to 70 degrees from horizontal — more upright than a standard bent over row.
Let the bar hang at arm’s length. Brace your core and lock in your back angle.
Row the bar to your lower abdomen by driving your elbows back along your sides. Keep elbows close to your body.
Squeeze your lats and lower traps at the top. Pause briefly.
Lower the bar under control. Maintain the same torso angle throughout.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Underhand grip shifts emphasis to lower lats and biceps
Builds back thickness more than back width
More upright torso is easier on the lower back
Allows heavier loading than standard bent over rows for many lifters
Popularized by Dorian Yates for building a legendary back
Excellent complement to overhand rowing variations

description.en: The barbell squat to shoulder press (barbell thruster) combines a front squat with an overhead press in one fluid movement. You squat down with the bar in the front rack, then stand and use the leg drive momentum to press the bar overhead. It is one of the most effective full-body conditioning exercises.

en: Set a barbell at front-rack height. Clean it to your front shoulders or unrack.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, bar in front rack.
Squat down to parallel or below.
Drive through your feet to stand explosively.
Use the standing momentum to press the bar overhead.
Lock out overhead.
Lower the bar back to the front rack as you descend into the next squat.
Move fluidly. Aim for 8 to 15 reps per set.
Full-body compound movement
Builds legs, shoulders, and core together
Excellent metabolic conditioning
CrossFit staple movement
Time-efficient
Develops leg drive and pressing coordination

description.en: The barbell strict curl is a curl variation performed with the back pressed against a wall to eliminate any swing or body english. The wall forces the biceps to do all the work without help from the lower back or hips. It is a punishing test of pure curl strength.

en: Stand with your back flat against a wall.
Hold a barbell with an underhand, shoulder-width grip.
Press your head, shoulders, and butt against the wall.
Let the barbell hang at thigh level.
Brace your core and keep your elbows tucked at your sides.
Curl the bar up to shoulder level using only your biceps.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the bar back to the start with control.
Eliminates body english
Pure biceps isolation
Builds true curl strength
Strong test of bicep power
Useful for strict-curl competitions
Improves arm strength

description.en: The bodyweight standing one arm row is a single arm horizontal row that uses a sturdy support. The lifter grips with one hand, leans back, and rows the chest toward the support. It builds back strength and trains each side independently using only body weight.

en: Stand in front of a sturdy upright support.
Grip the support with one hand at chest height.
Lean back with the arm straight and feet planted.
Brace your core and keep the body straight.
Pinch the working shoulder blade back.
Pull the chest toward the support by bending the elbow.
Squeeze the lat and upper back at the top.
Lower with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
No equipment needed
Trains each side
Builds the lats
Strong row variation
Useful for travel
Builds the biceps

description.en: The cable curl is a bicep curl performed at a low cable pulley with a straight bar, EZ bar, or rope attachment. The cable provides constant tension throughout the entire range of motion, including the top and bottom positions where dumbbell and barbell curls lose tension. This makes it one of the most effective bicep exercises for hypertrophy.

en: Attach a straight bar, EZ bar, or rope handle to a low cable pulley.
Stand facing the cable machine with feet hip-width apart. Grip the bar with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Step back slightly so the cable is under tension with your arms fully extended. Stand tall.
Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and pin your elbows against your sides.
Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows. Keep your elbows pinned to your sides.
Continue until the bar reaches shoulder height. Squeeze your biceps hard for one second.
Lower the bar under control over two seconds. Maintain constant cable tension — do not let the weight stack touch down.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Constant cable tension throughout the entire range of motion
Loads the top and bottom positions better than free weights
Easy to load progressively in small increments
Multiple attachment options for different stimuli
Excellent for high-rep bicep finishing work
Easier to maintain strict form than free-weight curls

description.en: The cable kneeling shoulder press uses a cable handle pressed overhead from a tall kneeling position. The kneeling stance removes any leg drive while the cable provides constant tension throughout the range. The combination forces strict shoulder pressing with strong core engagement.

en: Set a cable to a low pulley with a single handle.
Kneel on the floor facing away from the cable, with the handle in your right hand.
Position the handle at shoulder level with elbow tucked.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to lock the hips.
Press the handle straight up overhead until your arm is fully extended.
Squeeze your shoulder at the top.
Lower the handle back to shoulder level with control.
Complete reps on one side, then switch arms.
Removes leg drive for strict shoulder work
Constant cable tension through the range
Strong glute and core engagement
Builds shoulder strength unilaterally
Tall kneeling challenges hip stability
Useful for shoulder hypertrophy

description.en: The cable lying curl is a bicep isolation exercise performed lying flat on the floor or a bench in front of a low cable pulley. The lying position places the bicep at a slight stretch throughout the curl, and the cable maintains constant tension. It is one of the most strict bicep isolation setups available.

en: Position a flat bench (or floor space) in front of a low cable pulley. Attach a straight bar.
Lie on your back on the bench (or floor) with your head closest to the cable.
Reach back overhead and grip the bar with an underhand grip.
Pull the bar down so your arms are extended straight back overhead, palms up. The cable should be under tension.
Pin your upper arms — they will angle slightly back overhead. Keep them still.
Curl the bar by bending at the elbows. Squeeze your biceps as the bar moves toward your forehead.
Lower under control. Maintain cable tension and upper arm position.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Constant cable tension throughout the range
Lying position eliminates all body english
Slight bicep stretch loaded throughout
Excellent strict isolation exercise
Useful for high-rep bicep finishing
Easy to load progressively

description.en: The cable one arm lateral bent over is a unilateral rear delt fly done with a low cable. The lifter hinges forward and raises one arm out to the side. The cable provides constant tension on the rear delts throughout.

en: Set a cable to a low position with a single handle attached.
Stand sideways to the cable in a hinged position.
Grip the handle with the arm that crosses the body.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Raise the arm out to the side away from the body.
Keep a slight bend in the elbow throughout.
Squeeze the rear delt hard at the top.
Lower with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Targets the rear delts
Constant cable tension
Strong unilateral move
Builds shoulder shape
Useful rear delt builder

description.en: The cable one-arm reverse fly is a rear-delt isolation exercise performed at a low or mid-height cable pulley with a single-handle attachment. Training one arm at a time exposes left-right imbalances and allows greater focus on the contracting rear delt. The cable provides constant tension throughout the range.

en: Set a cable pulley to roughly waist or mid-torso height. Attach a D-handle.
Stand sideways to the cable. Reach across your body with the far hand and grip the handle.
Step back slightly. Set a slight bend in your working elbow and lock it in.
Brace your core. Stand tall or lean slightly forward.
Pull the handle out and back in a wide arc away from the cable, squeezing your rear delt.
Continue until your arm is roughly in line with your shoulder. Squeeze hard at the peak.
Slowly return under control. Maintain cable tension throughout.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
Constant cable tension throughout the full range
Trains one rear delt at a time for focus and balance
Exposes left-right imbalances
Easy to load progressively
Excellent finisher for shoulder or back days
Trains core anti-rotation as a secondary benefit

description.en: The cable one-arm tricep pushdown is a unilateral isolation exercise performed at a high cable pulley with a single-handle attachment. Training one arm at a time exposes and corrects left-right imbalances, allows greater range of motion than the two-arm version, and lets you focus completely on contracting one tricep. It is excellent for building the lateral head of the tricep.

en: Attach a single-handle (D-handle) to a high cable pulley.
Stand facing the cable machine with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the handle with your right hand using an overhand or neutral grip.
Pin your right elbow against your right side. Your forearm should start parallel to the floor or slightly higher.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Your free hand can rest on your hip for stability.
Push the handle straight down by extending only at the elbow. Keep your upper arm completely still.
Continue pushing until your arm is fully extended. Squeeze your tricep hard for one second at the bottom.
Slowly let the handle travel back up under control until your forearm is parallel to the floor again.
Complete all reps on the right side, then switch.
Exposes and corrects left-right tricep strength imbalances
Allows greater range of motion than the two-arm cable pushdown
Constant tension throughout the entire range
Easier to feel the target muscle than during bilateral work
Builds the lateral head of the tricep heavily
Easy to load progressively with small increments

description.en: The cable seated rear delt fly with chest support uses a bench tipped forward against an incline. Two cables pulled in by the arms sweep out to the sides for a strict isolation of the rear delts.

en: Set up an incline bench between two low cable pulleys.
Sit chest down against the incline pad.
Reach down and grab the opposite handle with each hand so the cables cross.
Brace the core and keep the chest pressed to the pad.
Sweep the arms out to the sides by squeezing the shoulder blades.
Stop at shoulder height with the elbows slightly bent.
Squeeze the rear delts at the top.
Lower the arms back down with control and repeat.
Isolates the rear delts and upper back.
Chest support eliminates body english.
Cable provides constant tension throughout.
Carryover to face pulls and pulling strength.
Builds upper back posture.
Easy to scale by adjusting cable weight.

description.en: The cable seated twist is a rotational core exercise performed seated facing perpendicular to a cable machine, holding a D-handle. You rotate your torso away from the cable, training rotational core strength against constant tension. It is similar to a Russian twist but with smoother resistance.

en: Set a cable pulley to roughly chest height. Attach a D-handle.
Sit on a bench facing perpendicular to the cable machine. Cable should be on your left.
Grip the handle with both hands. Extend your arms straight out in front of your chest.
Sit tall with chest lifted. Brace your core.
Rotate your torso to the right, away from the cable. Use your obliques to drive the rotation.
Keep your arms straight and elbows locked. The handle should travel through a smooth arc.
Pause briefly at the end of the rotation. Slowly return to the start.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch the cable to your right side.
Trains rotational core strength against constant tension
Smoother than Russian twists with weights
Easy to load progressively
Builds the obliques effectively
Useful for rotational sports (golf, tennis, baseball)
Standing variation also possible

description.en: The cable standing single arm fly is performed with a single D-handle on a cable, sweeping one arm across the body in a fly motion. Working one side at a time allows full focus on each chest and a deeper stretch through the working pec. It is a great accessory for chest detail and shape.

en: Set a cable to about shoulder height.
Attach a single D-handle to the cable.
Stand to one side of the machine, holding the handle in the far hand.
Step forward slightly to add tension.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
With a slight bend in the elbow, sweep your arm across your body.
Bring the hand to the centerline in front of your chest.
Squeeze the chest hard at the end range. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Strict unilateral chest work
Constant cable tension
Deep stretch through the pec
Helps fix chest imbalances
Builds chest shape and detail
Strong peak contraction

description.en: The chair leg extended stretch is a seated hamstring stretch performed in a chair where you extend one leg straight forward with the heel on the floor and hinge forward over it. It is convenient for office settings and accessible for anyone who cannot get to the floor easily.

en: Sit on the edge of a sturdy chair with both feet flat on the floor.
Extend your right leg straight forward with the heel on the floor and toes pointing up.
Sit up tall with chest lifted.
Place your hands on your right thigh.
Hinge forward at the hips over your right leg, keeping your back flat.
Slide your hands down your thigh toward your right foot.
Feel the stretch through your right hamstring.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Switch legs and repeat.
Stretches the hamstring of the extended leg
Convenient for office settings
Accessible for anyone who can sit in a chair
No equipment needed besides a chair
Quick and easy
Useful for desk workers

description.en: The corkscrew push-up adds a rotational twist during the push-up — as you lower, you rotate your body to one side, creating a spiraling or corkscrew motion. It builds pressing strength with rotational core demand.

en: Get into a push-up position.
As you lower, rotate your body to the right — your right shoulder dips lower.
Press back up while unrotating.
On the next rep, rotate to the left.
Continue alternating the rotation direction.
The rotation adds oblique and core demand.
Maintain controlled movement throughout.
Aim for 8 to 12 total reps.
Adds rotational core demand to push-ups
Spiraling motion targets the chest differently
No equipment needed
Engaging and unique variation
Builds oblique strength during pressing
Develops body control

description.en: The crane pose bakasana is a foundational yoga arm balance where the body balances on the hands with the knees resting high on the upper arms. The pose builds wrist, forearm, and core strength while teaching balance and body control.

en: Squat down with feet together and place your palms flat on the floor.
Set your hands shoulder-width apart in front of you.
Plant the fingers wide for stability.
Bring your knees up to rest high on the back of your upper arms.
Lean forward slowly to shift weight to the hands.
Lift one foot off the floor briefly to find balance.
Lift both feet off the floor when ready, balancing on the hands.
Hold the balance with the gaze forward then lower the feet down.
Builds wrist and forearm strength
Trains balance and body control
Strong yoga arm balance
No equipment needed
Useful core builder
Improves coordination

description.en: The dumbbell bent-over face pull is a rear deltoid exercise performed bent over where you pull dumbbells up toward your face with elbows high and wide. It targets the rear delts, rhomboids, and upper traps. It mimics the cable face pull with dumbbells.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold dumbbells with a neutral grip.
Hinge at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees to the floor.
Let the dumbbells hang with arms extended.
Row the dumbbells up toward your face by driving your elbows up and wide.
End with elbows at shoulder height or higher, dumbbells near your face.
Squeeze your rear delts and upper traps at the top.
Lower under control.
Use light to moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Targets the rear delts and upper traps
Mimics cable face pull with dumbbells
Builds posture and shoulder balance
No cable machine needed
Simple setup
Excellent warm-up or isolation exercise

description.en: The dumbbell bridge bench press combines a glute bridge hold with a dumbbell pressing movement. While holding your hips up in a bridge, you press dumbbells over your chest. This builds the chest and triceps while requiring the glutes and hamstrings to maintain the bridge position.

en: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat, holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Drive through your heels to lift your hips off the floor into a glute bridge position.
Maintain the bridge with your shoulders, hips, and knees in a straight line.
Hold the dumbbells at chest level with palms facing forward and elbows on the floor or just above.
Press both dumbbells straight up until your arms are fully extended.
Squeeze your chest and triceps at the top.
Lower the dumbbells with control until your elbows are back near the floor.
Hold the bridge throughout the entire set, only lowering after the final rep.
Trains chest and glutes simultaneously
Builds isometric glute and hamstring endurance
No bench required
Limited range of motion is shoulder-friendly
Forces total-body tension
Practical for home or floor training
Develops core stability under load

description.en: The dumbbell decline lying leg curl is a creative way to train the hamstrings without a leg curl machine. Lying face down on a decline bench with a dumbbell held between the feet, you curl the dumbbell up by flexing the knees. The decline angle and gravity create a strong hamstring contraction.

en: Set a bench to a decline angle.
Place a dumbbell in front of the bench at the high end.
Lie face down on the decline bench with hips at the high end.
Have a partner help place the dumbbell vertically between your feet.
Squeeze your feet together to hold the dumbbell securely.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Curl the dumbbell up by flexing your knees as far as possible.
Squeeze your hamstrings at the top, then lower with control.
Trains hamstrings without a machine
Decline angle increases the stretch
Builds hamstring strength and size
Useful at home with limited equipment
Develops grip strength in the feet
Strong eccentric load with the slow lowering

description.en: The dumbbell hang power clean uses two dumbbells starting at mid-thigh (hang position) and explosively drives them to the front rack using hip extension. The "power" designation means catching in a partial squat. It is easier to learn than barbell cleans and builds explosive power.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at mid-thigh.
Hinge at the hips slightly — dumbbells at the hang position.
Explosively extend hips, knees, and ankles — driving the dumbbells up.
As the dumbbells rise, pull yourself under them and rotate your elbows around.
Catch in a quarter-squat with the dumbbells on your front shoulders.
Stand up from the quarter-squat.
Lower back to the hang position and repeat.
Easier to learn than barbell cleans. Use moderate weight.
Builds explosive hip drive with dumbbells
Easier to learn than barbell variants
Develops catching mechanics
Excellent athletic power exercise
Builds bilateral coordination
Full-body movement

description.en: The dumbbell lateral-to-front raise combines a lateral raise with a front raise in one continuous motion. You raise the dumbbells to the sides (lateral), then sweep them forward (front), then lower. This targets both the lateral and anterior deltoid heads in one movement.

en: Stand with dumbbells at your sides, palms facing in.
Raise both dumbbells out to the sides to shoulder height (lateral raise).
From the top of the lateral raise, sweep the dumbbells forward in front of you (so arms now point forward at shoulder height).
Lower the dumbbells from the front position back to your sides.
That is one rep. Continue for the desired reps.
Move with control throughout the arc.
Use light weight — the continuous arc is demanding.
Aim for 8 to 10 reps.
Targets lateral and anterior delts in one movement
Time-efficient shoulder exercise
Extended time under tension through the arc
Light weight is very effective
Engaging and challenging variation
Builds complete shoulder development

description.en: The dumbbell RDL and bent over row pairs a full RDL hip hinge with a row at the bottom position. The combo trains the hamstrings, glutes, and entire upper back in one efficient move. It is a great workout for posterior chain strength and hypertrophy.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Hold the dumbbells at your thighs with palms facing your body.
Brace your core and keep a slight bend in the knees.
Hinge at the hips and lower the dumbbells along your legs.
Continue until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings.
In the bottom hinged position, row both dumbbells up to your ribs.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of the row.
Lower the dumbbells back down, then drive your hips forward to stand.
Trains the entire posterior chain
Time-efficient combo
Builds hamstring and back strength together
Improves hip hinge pattern
Useful for full body workouts
Strong hypertrophy move

description.en: The dumbbell reverse grip incline bench two-arm row is a chest-supported row performed lying face down on an incline bench with a supinated (underhand) grip. The chest support eliminates body english, and the underhand grip shifts more work to the biceps and lower lats.

en: Set an incline bench to 30 to 45 degrees. Lie face down with your chest on the pad and feet on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand with a supinated (underhand) grip, arms hanging straight down.
Row both dumbbells up toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back along your sides.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower under control over two seconds.
The chest support eliminates all momentum — every rep is strict.
Keep your chin above the top of the bench. Breathe steadily.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Strict isolation — chest support eliminates body english
Supinated grip targets lower lats and biceps
Easy on the lower back
Builds back thickness
Easy to load progressively
Excellent for hypertrophy

description.en: The dumbbell seated alternate front raise performs the front raise one arm at a time from a seated position. The seated position eliminates lower body cheating while the alternating pattern increases time under tension on each side. It is one of the strictest possible front raise variations.

en: Sit on a bench with a vertical back support and feet flat on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing back.
Sit tall with chest up.
Brace your core.
Maintain a slight bend in the elbows throughout.
Raise the right dumbbell forward to shoulder height while keeping the left at the side.
Squeeze the right front delt at the top, then lower with control.
Repeat with the left arm. Alternate sides each rep.
Strict single-arm front delt work
Seated position eliminates body english
Alternating pattern increases time under tension
Corrects left-right imbalances
Builds front delt size
Useful for hypertrophy training

description.en: The dumbbell single-leg hip thrust adds dumbbell loading to a single-leg hip thrust performed with upper back on a bench. One leg works while the other is extended forward. The per-glute demand is roughly double the bilateral version.

en: Sit with upper back against a bench. Place a dumbbell on your right hip crease.
Hold the dumbbell in place with your right hand.
Bend your right knee with foot flat. Extend your left leg straight forward or up.
Drive through your right heel to thrust your hips up.
At the top, body forms a straight line from right knee to shoulders.
Squeeze your right glute hard.
Lower under control.
Complete reps, then switch sides. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Progressive glute loading per leg
Exposes glute imbalances
Builds unilateral hip extension power
Excellent for glute hypertrophy
Easier to set up than barbell hip thrusts
Useful for athletic training

description.en: The dumbbell step-up lunge is a compound lower-body exercise that combines a weighted step-up with a reverse lunge. After stepping up onto a box, you step back down into a reverse lunge before reversing the movement. It builds unilateral leg strength and trains balance under load.

en: Stand facing a sturdy box or bench (knee-height) with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Step your right foot up onto the box. Drive through your right foot to stand fully on top.
From standing on top of the box, step your left foot back down behind you into a reverse lunge.
Lower your left knee toward the floor in the reverse lunge.
Drive through your right foot to step the left foot back up onto the box.
Step the right foot back down to the floor. That is one rep.
Complete all reps on the right, then switch sides.
Use moderate weight — the combination is more demanding than each exercise alone.
Combines step-up and reverse lunge for unilateral leg work
Builds quad and glute strength with balance demand
Exposes left-right imbalances
Time-efficient compound exercise
Trains coordination and proprioception
Works with one pair of dumbbells

description.en: The dumbbell twisted fly is a chest fly variation where you rotate your wrists at the top of the fly so your palms face each other and the dumbbell ends touch. The wrist rotation adds an extra inner chest squeeze at peak contraction.

en: Lie on a flat bench holding dumbbells above your chest with palms facing each other.
Maintain a slight bend in your elbows.
Lower both dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc until you feel a stretch in your chest.
Pull the dumbbells back up in an arc.
At the top, rotate your wrists slightly inward so the dumbbell heads touch — knuckles face down.
Squeeze your inner chest hard at the peak.
Lower under control back to the stretched position.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Wrist twist adds inner chest squeeze
Builds chest peak contraction
Standard fly with bonus contraction
Easy to load progressively
Different stimulus from standard fly
Engaging variation

description.en: The dumbbell V-up is a loaded V-up variation where you hold a dumbbell with both hands overhead and perform the simultaneous leg-and-torso lift to meet in the middle. The added load makes the V-up significantly more demanding, building serious ab strength.

en: Lie flat on your back with arms extended overhead, holding a dumbbell with both hands.
Extend your legs straight on the floor.
Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor.
Simultaneously lift your straight legs and your torso up to meet in a V-shape.
Reach the dumbbell toward your toes at the top.
Squeeze your abs hard at the peak.
Slowly lower back to the start position over two seconds. Keep the dumbbell controlled.
Use light weight to start. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per set.
Adds loading to V-ups for progressive overload
Builds elite ab strength
Trains hip flexors
Easy to scale by dumbbell weight
Useful when bodyweight V-ups are too easy
Time-efficient core exercise

description.en: The exercise ball back extension with hands behind head is a back extension done over a stability ball with the hands placed behind the head. The hand position adds slight load to the upper body and helps maintain a neutral neck position.

en: Lie face down with the hips supported on a stability ball.
Set the feet wide on the floor for stability.
Place the hands behind the head with elbows wide.
Brace the core and keep the body relaxed at the start.
Lift the chest off the ball by extending the back.
Continue lifting until the body forms a straight line.
Squeeze the lower back and glutes at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
Builds the lower back.
Trains the glutes.
Hands behind head adds challenge.
Joint friendly back work.
Useful for posture.

description.en: The front plank walkout starts in a standing position, then walks the hands forward into a plank and back to standing. The dynamic motion challenges the core through the entire walkout pattern and builds shoulder and chest endurance. It is a strong full body warmup or core conditioning exercise.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Hinge at the hips and place your hands on the floor in front of your feet.
Walk your hands forward one at a time.
Continue walking forward until you reach a high plank position.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Hold the plank briefly with body in a straight line.
Walk your hands back toward your feet.
Stand back up and repeat.
Builds core stability through motion
Strong shoulder endurance challenge
Develops body control
No equipment required
Useful for warmups
Total body coordination

description.en: The front to side plank is a dynamic core exercise where you alternate between a forearm front plank and a forearm side plank, rotating your body to switch positions. It trains anti-extension (front plank) and anti-lateral-flexion (side plank) in one continuous movement, building well-rounded core strength.

en: Begin in a forearm plank position — elbows under shoulders, body in a straight line, core braced.
Hold the front plank for 2 to 3 seconds.
Rotate your body to the right, lifting your right arm toward the ceiling and stacking your feet for a side plank on your left elbow.
Hold the side plank for 2 to 3 seconds. Keep your hips lifted.
Rotate back to the front plank position.
Then rotate to the left side for a side plank on your right elbow.
Continue alternating sides through the front plank.
Perform for time (30 to 60 seconds) or for a target number of rotations.
Trains anti-extension and anti-lateral-flexion in one movement
Builds well-rounded core strength
Develops shoulder stability through transitions
Time-efficient core exercise
No equipment needed
Excellent for athletes

description.en: The high knee run is a cardiovascular conditioning exercise where you run in place (or moving forward) while driving your knees as high as possible with each step. It builds hip flexor strength, cardiovascular conditioning, and running mechanics. It is a staple warm-up and HIIT exercise.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Arms at your sides.
Begin running in place, driving your right knee up toward your chest as high as possible.
As your right foot lands, immediately drive your left knee up.
Pump your arms in opposition to your legs — right arm swings forward as left knee rises, and vice versa.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Land softly with each step.
Move as quickly as possible while maintaining form. Knees should reach at least hip height.
Keep your torso upright — do not lean forward.
Perform for time (20 to 45 seconds) or distance.
Excellent cardiovascular conditioning
Builds hip flexor strength and endurance
Improves running mechanics and knee drive
No equipment needed — works anywhere
Time-efficient warm-up or HIIT exercise
Increases heart rate rapidly

description.en: The hip raise bridge is essentially the standard glute bridge — lying on your back and thrusting your hips upward. This is the most basic glute activation exercise and is foundational for all hip thrust variations.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart.
Arms at your sides, palms down.
Drive through your heels to lift your hips up.
At the top, your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Squeeze your glutes hard. Hold for 1 to 2 seconds.
Lower under control.
Do not hyperextend your lower back.
Aim for 15 to 20 reps per set.
Most basic glute activation exercise
Foundational for all hip thrust variations
No equipment needed
Builds glute activation awareness
Supports lower back health
Beginner-friendly

description.en: The human flag is an elite-level calisthenic skill where you hold your body horizontally to the side of a vertical pole, supported only by your hands gripping the pole. It demands elite shoulder strength, lat power, and core control. It is one of the most impressive bodyweight skills possible.

en: Find a sturdy vertical pole that can support your weight. Stand sideways to it.
Grip the pole with both hands stacked vertically — top hand higher with overhand grip pulling down, bottom hand lower pushing the pole away.
The top hand pulls toward you while the bottom hand pushes away — creating opposing forces.
Brace your core hard. Engage your lats.
Lift your legs off the ground and extend them out to the side, parallel to the floor.
Your body forms a horizontal “flag” parallel to the ground.
Hold for as long as possible — even 1 to 5 seconds is impressive at first.
This is elite-level. Build up with tuck flags, single-leg flags, and progressive holds first.
Builds elite shoulder, lat, and core strength
Develops complete body control
Impressive calisthenic skill
Trains opposing force production
Carries over to all advanced bodyweight skills
Builds mental toughness and dedication

description.en: The jack split crunches combine a crunch with a split leg motion that mimics the leg portion of a jumping jack. As you crunch up, you simultaneously split the legs out wide, then bring them back together as you lower. The combination keeps the abs engaged through both upper and lower body movement.

en: Lie on your back with legs extended together and arms at your sides.
Brace your abs hard.
Crunch your shoulders off the floor.
At the same time, split your legs out wide to either side.
Reach your hands toward the outside of your legs.
Squeeze the abs at the top.
Lower your shoulders back down as you bring the legs back together.
Continue at a steady pace.
Combines crunch with leg split
Strong full ab engagement
No equipment required
Builds adductor strength
Different stimulus than standard crunches
Useful for ab training

description.en: The jump on fit box is a box jump done onto a sturdy fit box or plyo box. The lifter jumps from the floor to the top of the box with both feet. It is a strong explosive leg power builder.

en: Stand in front of a sturdy fit box.
Set the feet shoulder width apart.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Bend the knees and swing the arms back.
Drive through the feet and swing the arms up.
Jump up onto the top of the box.
Land soft with knees bent on top of the box.
Step down and reset for the next rep.
Builds leg power
Strong explosive move
Trains the legs
Useful for athletes
Burns calories
Builds the glutes

description.en: The kettlebell lying on floor single arm bottoms up chest press is a stability focused press from the floor with an inverted bell. The bottoms up position turns the press into a serious grip and shoulder stabilizer drill.

en: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat.
Hold a kettlebell upside down with one hand at chest level.
Squeeze the handle hard to keep the bell balanced.
Brace the core and tuck the working elbow at about 45 degrees.
Press the kettlebell straight up over your shoulder.
Keep the wrist neutral and the bell perfectly vertical.
Lower the kettlebell back to the floor with full control.
Complete all reps on one side then switch arms.
Demands elite grip and forearm strength.
Builds chest and shoulder stability under unstable load.
Floor position limits over reaching for shoulder safety.
Trains the rotator cuff and small stabilizers.
Single arm work corrects imbalances.
Excellent grip drill with light loads.

description.en: The kettlebell side lunge is a lateral lunge variation where you hold a kettlebell at your chest (goblet position) while stepping out to the side and squatting down on the working leg. The lateral motion targets the adductors, gluteus medius, and quads. The kettlebell adds load and core demand.

en: Hold a kettlebell at your chest with both hands (goblet position). Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Step your right foot out wide to the right.
Bend your right knee and sit your right hip back. Keep your left leg straight.
Lower your hips toward your right heel. Your right thigh should approach parallel.
Keep your chest up and back flat. The kettlebell stays at your chest.
Push through your right foot to return to standing. Bring the right foot back to the starting position.
Repeat on the left side. Continue alternating.
Move with control. Use moderate weight to start.
Builds adductor, glute, and quad strength laterally
Adds load to the lateral lunge pattern
Improves hip mobility and balance
Trains anti-rotation core stability
Excellent warm-up or accessory for squats
Carries over to lateral athletic movement

description.en: The kneeling abdominal draw in is a deep core activation drill done on all fours. The mover pulls the navel toward the spine while keeping the back flat. It builds transverse abdominis strength and core control.

en: Set up on hands and knees in a quadruped position.
Place the hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips.
Keep the back flat and head neutral.
Brace your core and inhale to expand the belly.
Exhale and pull the navel up toward the spine.
Hold the draw in position briefly.
Release and let the belly expand naturally.
Continue for the working set.
Builds the deep core
Trains the transverse abdominis
Strong core activation
Useful for posture
Builds core control

description.en: The kneeling back rotation stretch (also called Thread the Needle) is a thoracic spine mobility drill performed on hands and knees where you reach one arm under your body, then up and overhead, rotating through the upper back. It is one of the most effective drills for thoracic rotation mobility.

en: Start on your hands and knees in tabletop position.
Reach your right arm up toward the ceiling, opening your chest to the right. Look up at your right hand.
Then reach your right arm down and underneath your left armpit, rotating your torso.
Lower your right shoulder and the right side of your head to the floor.
Continue alternating: reaching up and over, then down and through.
Feel the rotation through your thoracic spine and stretch through your shoulder.
Move slowly with breath control. Inhale up, exhale through.
Perform 5 to 8 reps per side.
Mobilizes the thoracic spine through rotation
Stretches the rear shoulders and rhomboids
Excellent warm-up for upper-body training
Easier on the lower back than standing rotations
No equipment needed
Useful for shoulder mobility too

description.en: The lever parallel chest press is performed on a leverage chest press machine with parallel (neutral grip) handles. The neutral grip reduces shoulder strain compared to pronated handles while the machine fixed path eliminates balance demands. It is a shoulder-friendly chest builder.

en: Sit at a leverage chest press machine with parallel handles.
Adjust the seat so the handles align with your mid chest.
Grip the parallel handles with palms facing each other.
Pull your shoulders back and brace your core.
Press the handles forward until your arms are fully extended.
Squeeze your chest at the top.
Lower the handles back to chest level with control.
Maintain the neutral grip throughout the entire set.
Neutral grip is shoulder-friendly
Fixed motion path eliminates balance demands
Builds chest size and strength
Useful for sensitive shoulders
Allows progressive heavy loading
Beginner-friendly chest variation

description.en: The medicine ball single-leg deadlift performs a single-leg Romanian deadlift while holding a medicine ball as a light counterbalance and load. The med ball provides enough weight to challenge the hinge while serving as a counterbalance for better single-leg balance.

en: Stand on your right leg holding a medicine ball in front of you.
Hinge at the right hip — push your left leg straight behind you.
Lower the med ball toward the floor as your torso descends.
Continue until you feel a hamstring stretch.
Drive through your right hip to stand back up.
The med ball serves as both load and counterbalance.
Complete reps, then switch legs.
Aim for 8 to 12 reps per leg.
Light loading with counterbalance benefit
Builds single-leg hinge strength
Develops balance and proprioception
Med ball is easier to hold than dumbbells for beginners
Useful for warm-up or accessory work
Accessible and simple

description.en: The mountain climber lunge is a dynamic conditioning exercise where you start in a high plank and bring one foot up next to the corresponding hand (like a deep lunge stretch), then alternate sides. It combines core stability with hip mobility and cardiovascular conditioning.

en: Start in a high plank position. Hands under shoulders, body straight from heels to head.
Bring your right foot forward and place it flat on the floor next to your right hand (or as close as you can get).
Hold briefly in the deep lunge stretch position.
Step your right foot back to the plank.
Bring your left foot forward to the outside of your left hand. Hold briefly.
Step the left foot back. Continue alternating.
Maintain a strong plank throughout. Do not let your hips sag.
Move at a moderate pace — control matters more than speed.
Combines core stability with hip mobility
Stretches the hip flexors dynamically
Cardiovascular conditioning
Builds shoulder endurance
No equipment needed
Excellent dynamic warm-up

description.en: The one-leg donkey calf raise performs donkey calf raises (bent at the waist) on a single leg. The bent-over position and single-leg loading create significant gastrocnemius demand. A partner can sit on your lower back for added load.

en: Stand on a step with the ball of your right foot on the edge. Bend at the waist and support yourself on a bench or rack.
Tuck your left foot behind your right ankle.
Lower your right heel as far as possible for a full stretch.
Press through the ball of your foot to raise as high as possible.
Squeeze your calf at the top.
Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch legs.
A partner can sit on your lower back for added load.
Aim for 15 to 20 reps per leg.
Doubles the calf demand per leg
Bent-over position targets the gastrocnemius
Partner can add load by sitting on your back
Exposes left-right calf imbalances
No machine needed
Unique old-school calf exercise

description.en: The pulse row is a bodyweight inverted row variation where you hold at the top of the row and perform small pulsing reps (2 to 3 inches of movement) rather than full range reps. The pulsing keeps constant peak tension on the lats and mid-back, building endurance and mind-muscle connection.

en: Set up an inverted row position — hang from a bar or TRX at hip height, body in a straight line.
Row yourself up to the bar so your chest is near the bar.
At the top, perform small pulsing reps — lower 2 to 3 inches and pull back up.
Maintain the near-top position throughout — never fully extend.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together on each pulse.
Continue pulsing for the desired reps or time.
Maintain a straight body line throughout.
Aim for 15 to 25 pulses per set.
Constant peak tension on the back
Builds endurance and mind-muscle connection
Excellent finisher exercise
No additional equipment needed
Develops isometric back strength
Engaging variation on standard rows

description.en: The push press is an overhead pressing variation that uses a brief, powerful dip-and-drive of the legs to help launch the bar past the shoulders. The leg drive lets you press significantly heavier loads than a strict press, building overhead strength and explosive power. It is a foundational lift in CrossFit, Olympic weightlifting, and athletic performance training.

en: Stand with the loaded barbell racked across your front shoulders, hands just outside shoulder-width, elbows up.
Set your feet hip-width apart with toes pointed straight ahead.
Brace your core hard and lift your chest tall.
Initiate the dip by bending only at the knees — about 10 to 15 cm (4 to 6 inches). Keep your torso completely vertical. Do not bend at the hips.
Reverse the dip explosively by driving through your feet and extending your hips and knees.
As your legs reach full extension, press the bar straight up overhead. The leg drive does most of the work; your arms finish the lift.
Lock out with the bar directly over your shoulders and head, arms fully extended.
Lower the bar under control back to the front rack position. Reset your dip and drive for the next rep.
Allows you to press significantly more weight overhead than a strict press
Builds explosive lower-body power and full-body coordination
Trains the core and lower body to transmit force through the upper body
Excellent crossover to Olympic lifting and athletic performance
Builds total-body strength and conditioning in one movement
Useful when shoulder strict press strength is the limiting factor

description.en: The push through reach is a quadruped mobility and core drill performed on the hands and knees. The lifter reaches one arm forward and threads it under the body in a smooth motion. The reach mobilizes the shoulders and trains the core to resist rotation.

en: Get on your hands and knees in a tabletop position.
Set the hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Lift one hand off the floor.
Reach the arm forward and through the gap under the body.
Continue the reach to the opposite side.
Pull the arm back through to the start.
Repeat reaches alternating arms.
Mobilizes the shoulders
Trains anti-rotation core
No equipment needed
Useful warm-up drill
Easy mobility move
Strong core builder

description.en: The resistance band inverted row adds band tension to a bodyweight inverted row by looping a band across your chest or holding it during the row. The band provides extra resistance at the top of the row, making an already-challenging exercise even harder for advanced trainees.

en: Set up a bar at hip height (in a power rack or sturdy table).
Loop a resistance band across your chest (over your back, under the bar).
Hang from the bar with arms extended, body in a straight line from heels to head.
Row your chest toward the bar by driving your elbows down and back.
The band adds resistance, making the row harder especially at the top.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower under control.
Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Adds progressive overload to inverted rows
Builds back strength beyond bodyweight alone
Constant tension with band resistance
Useful for advanced at-home trainees
Easy to scale by band thickness
No additional equipment beyond a bar and band

description.en: The resistance band reverse crunch is a lower-ab exercise where you lie on your back with a resistance band looped around your feet (anchored at a low point) and pull your knees toward your chest by curling your hips off the floor. The band adds progressive resistance to the standard reverse crunch.

en: Anchor a band at a low point. Loop the other end around your feet.
Lie on your back with your head away from the anchor. Bend your knees to 90 degrees.
The band should be under tension at the start. Place your hands at your sides for stability.
Brace your core. Pull your knees toward your chest by curling your hips off the floor.
At the peak, your knees should be near your chest and your hips lifted slightly.
Squeeze your lower abs hard.
Lower under control back to the starting position. Maintain band tension throughout.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Adds progressive resistance to the reverse crunch
Targets the lower abs effectively
Easy to scale by changing band thickness
Highly portable
Useful when no cable machine is available
Constant tension throughout the range

description.en: Resistance band shoulder adduction is a lat isolation exercise where you anchor a band overhead, grip it with one hand, and pull your arm straight down to your side. The movement isolates the lats through shoulder adduction without involving the biceps, similar to a straight-arm pulldown.

en: Anchor a resistance band at a high point overhead.
Stand to one side of the anchor. Grip the band with your right hand, arm extended overhead.
Stand tall. Brace your core.
Pull your right arm straight down to your side against the band tension.
Keep your arm straight throughout (slight elbow bend only).
Squeeze your lat at the bottom when your arm is at your side.
Slowly let the band pull your arm back overhead.
Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Isolates the lats through shoulder adduction
Minimal bicep involvement
Constant band tension throughout
Highly portable
Easy to scale
Useful for lat activation or isolation

description.en: The roll ball trapezius upper is a self myofascial release drill for the upper trap. Pressing a ball into the upper trap at the top of the shoulder releases tightness from desk work and stress.

en: Stand with the back to a wall.
Place a massage ball between the upper trap and the wall.
Brace the core and keep the body tall.
Press into the ball with controlled pressure.
Roll the upper trap slowly across the ball.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Tip the head gently to deepen the release.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the upper trap.
Reduces neck tension.
Improves shoulder mobility.
Useful for desk workers.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The seated quadriceps stretch is performed kneeling with feet beside your hips, then leaning back gradually to deepen the quadriceps stretch. It is similar to a reclining hero pose. Going only as far back as your flexibility allows targets the quadriceps and hip flexors progressively.

en: Kneel on the floor with knees together and feet hip-width apart, tops of feet flat on the floor.
Sit back between your heels onto the floor (or onto a yoga block if you cannot reach the floor).
Place your hands on the floor behind you for support.
Gradually lean back, lowering yourself onto your forearms.
If your flexibility allows, continue to lower onto your back. Otherwise, stay on your forearms.
Feel the deep stretch through your quadriceps and hip flexors.
Hold for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe deeply.
To exit, push back up to seated, then carefully extend one leg at a time.
Deeply stretches the quadriceps
Stretches the hip flexors and ankles
Improves quad flexibility for squat depth
No equipment needed (block optional)
Excellent post-workout stretch for leg days
Works at home

description.en: The side plank is an isometric core exercise where you support your body sideways on one forearm and the side of one foot, holding a straight body line. It builds the obliques, quadratus lumborum, and lateral hip stabilizers. As an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, it teaches the core to resist sideways collapse — a critical pattern for athletic performance and lower-back health.

en: Lie on your right side with your right forearm flat on the floor, elbow directly under your shoulder.
Stack your left foot on top of your right foot, with legs straight.
Brace your core hard and lift your hips off the floor by pressing through your right forearm and the side of your right foot.
Form a straight line from your head to your heels. Your body should look like a sideways plank from any angle.
Pull your right shoulder away from your ear — do not let it shrug up. Place your left hand on your hip or extend it straight up.
Hold this position for the desired duration. Breathe normally throughout.
To finish, lower your hips back to the floor under control.
Switch sides and repeat. Aim for 20 to 60 seconds per side, building duration as you get stronger.
Builds the obliques and lateral core strength
Trains the core to resist sideways collapse (anti-lateral-flexion)
Improves hip stability and shoulder stability
Carries over to all lifts and athletic movements
No equipment needed — works anywhere
Excellent for lower-back health

description.en: The side sit-up lies on your side and performs a sit-up by laterally flexing your spine — lifting your torso off the floor sideways. It directly targets the obliques through lateral spinal flexion.

en: Lie on your right side. Stack your legs. Anchor your feet or have a partner hold them.
Place your left hand behind your head.
Laterally flex your spine — lift your torso off the floor sideways.
Rise as high as possible. Squeeze your left oblique.
Lower under control.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
This is a direct oblique exercise through lateral flexion.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Direct oblique loading through lateral flexion
Isolates one side at a time
No equipment needed
Builds oblique strength and definition
Simple and effective
Develops lateral core power

description.en: The sled calf press on leg press is a calf raise performed on the leg press machine. The lifter sits on the leg press, places the balls of the feet on the bottom edge of the platform, and presses the sled with just the calves. It allows heavy loading of the calves.

en: Sit on a leg press machine with the back flat against the pad.
Set the platform load with the appropriate weight.
Place the balls of the feet on the bottom edge of the platform.
Set the heels hanging off the edge.
Press the sled to extend the legs to almost lockout.
Brace your core and unrack the safeties.
Let the heels drop below the platform to stretch.
Press the platform up by rising onto the toes squeezing the calves.
Heavy calf builder
Easy to overload
Builds calf size
Useful calf builder
Strong machine move
Trains the gastrocnemius

description.en: Sphinx Pose is a gentle yoga backbend performed lying face down with the forearms pressed into the floor under the shoulders. It opens the chest and lengthens the spine while being significantly gentler than Cobra or Upward-Facing Dog. It is appropriate for beginners and for restorative practice.

en: Lie face down on the floor with legs extended and the tops of your feet pressing into the mat.
Place your forearms flat on the floor with elbows directly under your shoulders. Forearms parallel.
Press your forearms and pubic bone into the floor. Lift your chest and head.
Roll your shoulders back and down. Open your chest.
Engage your glutes gently to protect your lower back.
Look forward with a long neck — do not crank your head back.
Hold for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe deeply into your chest.
To exit, lower your chest and forehead back to the floor.
Gentle backbend appropriate for all levels
Opens the chest and front shoulders
Strengthens the lower back gently
Counteracts forward-hunched posture
Restorative and calming
Good preparation for deeper backbends

description.en: The standing figure four pose is a balance-challenging stretch where you cross one ankle over the opposite knee (creating a figure-four shape) and sit your hips back into a partial squat. It stretches the piriformis, deep hip rotators, and gluteus maximus of the crossed leg while training single-leg balance.

en: Stand tall on your left leg. Cross your right ankle over your left knee, resting it just above the kneecap.
Flex your right foot (pull toes toward shin) to protect the knee joint.
Sit your hips back and down as if sitting into a chair. Your left knee bends into a partial squat.
Keep your chest lifted and back flat. Use a wall or chair for balance if needed.
Gently press your right knee open to deepen the stretch in the right glute and hip.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Stand back up and switch sides.
Go only as deep as your flexibility allows — the stretch should be felt in the glute, not the knee.
Stretches the piriformis and deep hip rotators
Opens the glutes and outer hip
Trains single-leg balance simultaneously
Useful for relieving sciatic tension
No equipment needed — works anywhere
Practical standing stretch for between sets or at work

description.en: The standing one arm chest stretch uses a wall or sturdy post. With one arm placed against the wall and the body turning away, the chest and front shoulder open up on that side.

en: Stand next to a wall or sturdy post.
Place one hand on the wall behind you at shoulder height.
Keep the arm straight and the palm pressing the wall.
Plant the same side foot.
Brace the core and keep the chest tall.
Slowly turn the body away from the wall.
Feel the stretch across the front of the chest and shoulder.
Hold the stretch for the desired duration then switch sides.
Opens the chest and front shoulders one side at a time.
No equipment needed beyond a wall.
Easy to perform anywhere.
Improves shoulder mobility.
Carryover to overhead lifts and bench press.
Reduces tension from desk work.

description.en: The standing side stretch is a simple flexibility drill performed by standing tall, reaching one arm overhead, and bending sideways at the waist. It opens the obliques, intercostals, lats, and side body. It is one of the most accessible stretches for the upper body and works anywhere.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Arms at your sides.
Reach your right arm straight up overhead.
Bend your torso to the left, reaching your right arm up and over.
Keep your hips squared forward — do not push them out to the right.
Feel the stretch through your right side body, obliques, and lats.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Slowly return to upright. Switch sides and repeat.
Avoid leaning forward or backward — the stretch is purely lateral.
Opens the side body, obliques, and lats
Improves lateral spinal flexibility
Quick and accessible
Counteracts forward-hunched posture
No equipment needed
Excellent between-sets stretch

description.en: The stick twist lunge stretch combines a deep lunge with a thoracic spine rotation using a PVC stick or broomstick. Holding the stick across the upper back, you drop into a lunge and rotate the torso toward the front leg. The combination opens the hip flexors and increases thoracic mobility.

en: Hold a PVC stick or broomstick across your upper back.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Brace your core.
Step forward into a deep lunge with your right leg.
Lower your back knee toward the floor.
Press your back hip forward for a hip flexor stretch.
Rotate your torso to the right by twisting through the thoracic spine.
Hold the stretch, then return to center and switch sides.
Combines hip flexor and thoracic mobility
Strong hip flexor opening
Improves rotational mobility
Useful for warmups
Stick adds rotation reference
Stretches multiple muscle groups

description.en: The sumo squat floor touch performs a wide-stance (sumo) squat and reaches down to touch the floor between your feet at the bottom. The floor touch ensures consistent depth and adds a reaching component for hip mobility.

en: Stand with feet wide, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees.
Squat down by pushing your knees out and sitting your hips down.
At the bottom, reach down and touch the floor between your feet.
Drive through your feet to stand.
The floor touch ensures full depth every rep.
Keep your chest tall and back flat.
Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Useful as a warm-up or mobility drill.
Ensures consistent squat depth via floor touch
Builds hip mobility and adductor flexibility
No equipment needed
Useful warm-up exercise
Develops wide-stance squat depth
Simple and accessible

description.en: The superman push-up is an advanced plyometric push-up where you push off the floor with enough force that your entire body lifts off the ground, and you briefly extend your arms forward and legs back (like Superman flying) before landing back in the push-up position. It builds explosive upper-body power and total-body coordination.

en: Get into a standard push-up position. Hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, body in a straight line.
Lower your chest toward the floor in a controlled descent.
Explode upward with maximum force. Push hard enough that your hands AND feet leave the floor simultaneously.
While airborne, extend your arms forward and your legs back — forming a “Superman” flying position.
Quickly bring your hands and feet back to the push-up position before landing.
Land softly with slightly bent elbows and knees to absorb the impact.
Immediately drop into the next rep or reset your position.
This is an advanced explosive exercise. Master clap push-ups first. Use 1 to 5 reps per set.
Builds extreme upper-body explosive power
Trains total-body coordination
Develops fast-twitch muscle fibers
Impressive calisthenics skill
No equipment needed
Trains the core explosively

description.en: The supported headstand yoga pose, or Sirsasana, is an advanced inversion. With the forearms on the floor and the crown of the head between the hands, the body balances upside down to build full body strength.

en: Kneel on the floor and clasp the hands together.
Place the forearms on the floor with the elbows shoulder width apart.
Set the crown of the head on the floor with the hands cupping the back of the head.
Walk the feet toward the head until the hips stack over the shoulders.
Brace the core and lift one knee up at a time.
Slowly extend the legs straight up toward the ceiling.
Stack the feet over the hips and shoulders in a long line.
Hold the pose for the desired duration then come down with control.
Builds full body strength and balance.
Trains shoulder, core, and arm stability.
Improves proprioception upside down.
Calms the mind in classical yoga practice.
No equipment needed.
Considered the king of yoga poses.

description.en: The suspender front plank holds a plank position with the feet in suspension strap loops. The unstable straps force the core to work overtime to maintain a straight body line. It is a much more challenging variation of the standard plank and builds total core stability.

en: Adjust suspension straps to about a foot off the floor.
Place your feet inside the straps with toes hooked through.
Get into a high plank position with hands on the floor.
Position your hands shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes.
Hold a straight line from head to heels.
Resist the unstable straps trying to swing your feet around.
Hold for the duration without breaking form.
Maximizes core stability work
Strong shoulder stabilization
Builds anti-extension core strength
Different stimulus than standard plank
Develops body control
Useful for advanced core training

description.en: The suspender push up uses suspension straps with feet in the foot cradles. From a high plank position with feet suspended, you perform push ups while the unstable straps demand strong core and shoulder stabilization. It is one of the more challenging push up variations.

en: Anchor suspension straps overhead with the foot cradles hanging at calf height.
Place your feet in the foot cradles and assume a high plank position.
Set your hands shoulder-width apart on the floor.
Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes.
Lower your chest toward the floor by bending the elbows.
Continue down until your chest nearly touches the floor.
Press back up by extending your arms.
Maintain a straight body line and stable feet throughout.
Strong core and stability demand
Builds chest, triceps, and shoulders
Suspended feet challenge balance
Develops total body tension
Useful for breaking through push up plateaus
Excellent for home or travel training

description.en: The suspension trainer body saw is a TRX core move where the feet are placed in foot cradles and the body slides forward and back from a forearm plank position. The smooth saw motion challenges the abs and is a brutal core builder.

en: Set the suspension trainer foot cradles low.
Place the feet in the foot cradles facing down.
Set the forearms on the floor in a forearm plank.
Brace your core hard and keep the body in a straight line.
Slide the body forward by pushing through the forearms.
Slide the body back by pulling with the forearms.
Continue the saw motion forward and back with control.
Avoid letting the hips drop.
Brutal ab builder
Trains anti-extension core
Strong TRX move
No floor space needed
Builds shoulder stability
Useful core finisher

description.en: The transverse step-up steps onto a box from a lateral position and includes a rotation during the step. It builds multi-planar leg strength — combining the frontal (lateral step) and transverse (rotation) planes in one movement.

en: Stand to the side of a box or step.
Place your inside foot on the box.
Drive through that foot to step up onto the box, rotating your body to face forward as you rise.
Stand fully on the box.
Step back down to the side, unrotating.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
The rotation adds transverse plane demand.
Aim for 8 to 10 reps per side.
Multi-planar leg strength building
Combines lateral and rotational movement
Develops sport-specific movement patterns
Builds hip rotational control
No weights needed
Useful for athletes

description.en: The twist push up adds a torso rotation at the top of each push up. After pressing back up to the high plank, you rotate your torso to one side, lifting one arm up to point at the ceiling. The combination trains chest pressing along with rotational core strength in one efficient movement.

en: Get into a high plank position with hands shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes.
Lower your chest toward the floor by bending the elbows.
Press back up to the high plank position.
At the top, rotate your torso to the right and lift your right hand off the floor.
Reach your right hand up toward the ceiling, forming a side plank.
Hold the side plank briefly, then return your right hand to the floor.
Lower into the next push up. Alternate sides each rep.
Trains chest and obliques together
Strong rotational core demand
Builds total body coordination
Time-efficient compound movement
Develops shoulder stability
No equipment required

description.en: The weighted chin-up adds external load via a dip belt or weighted vest to the standard chin-up. The underhand grip places the biceps in a stronger position than the pull-up, often allowing more weight to be added. It is one of the best compound exercises for simultaneously building the lats and biceps with progressive overload.

en: Attach a weight plate to a dip belt and clip the belt around your waist. Alternatively, wear a weighted vest.
Reach up and grip a sturdy pull-up bar with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands roughly shoulder-width apart.
Hang with arms fully extended, feet off the floor. Cross your ankles behind you so the weight stays steady.
Pull your shoulder blades down and back. Brace your core hard.
Pull your body up by driving your elbows down toward your ribs. Lead with your chest.
Continue until your chin clears the bar. Squeeze your lats and biceps hard at the top.
Lower yourself slowly under control to a full hang with arms completely straight.
Add weight in small increments (2.5 to 10 lbs). Aim for 3 to 8 reps per set with weight.
Builds the lats and biceps with progressive overload
Stronger bicep position often allows more weight than pull-ups
Builds grip strength and shoulder stability under load
Strong predictor of relative upper-body strength
Direct carryover to all pulling strength
Develops core stability under loaded suspension

description.en: The weighted front raise is a front-delt isolation exercise where you hold a weight plate (or other weighted object like a sandbag or kettlebell) with both hands at your hips and lift it forward to shoulder height. The two-handed grip allows for slightly heavier loading than dumbbell front raises.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold a weight plate with both hands at your hips, gripping the sides of the plate.
Brace your core. Pull your shoulders back and down.
Lift the plate straight up in front of you with arms extended.
Maintain a slight bend in your elbows throughout.
Continue lifting until the plate reaches shoulder height.
Pause briefly. Squeeze your front delts.
Lower under control over two seconds back to your hips.
Use moderate weight. Avoid swinging.
Isolates the front deltoid
Two-handed grip allows heavier loading
Easy to set up at home
Builds front delt size and strength
No bench needed
Useful warm-up for pressing

description.en: The weighted kneeling step with swing is a dynamic transitional exercise that takes you from a half kneeling position up to a standing step while swinging a dumbbell overhead or forward. It strengthens the legs, hips, and core.

en: Hold a dumbbell with both hands in front of your hips.
Begin in a half kneeling position with one knee on the floor.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Drive through the front heel to stand up and step the back foot forward.
As you rise, swing the dumbbell up to chest or shoulder height.
Stand fully tall with the dumbbell at the top of the swing.
Step the working leg back and lower into the kneeling start.
Continue alternating sides for the desired number of reps.
Builds single leg strength through the kneeling to standing transition.
Trains hip drive and glute activation under load.
Strengthens the core to control the dumbbell swing.
Improves get up coordination useful for daily life.
Combines lower body work with shoulder mobility.
Loads the legs unilaterally to expose strength imbalances.

description.en: Wind sprints (standing arm sprints) are a conditioning exercise where you stand in place and pump your arms as fast as possible — mimicking sprint arm mechanics. It builds shoulder endurance, cardiovascular conditioning, and can be used as active recovery or a finisher.

en: Stand in a split stance, slightly bent at the waist.
Pump your arms as fast as possible — driving elbows back and forward like sprinting.
Hands should move from hip to chin level.
Maintain core bracing throughout.
Continue pumping at maximum speed for 15 to 30 seconds.
Rest briefly, then repeat.
Focus on speed over power.
Perform 3 to 5 rounds.
Builds shoulder endurance rapidly
Cardiovascular conditioning without running
No equipment needed
Useful for active recovery
Quick and intense
Builds arm speed

description.en: The X drill is an agility drill performed by running an X-shaped pattern between four cones placed in a square. You sprint diagonally to one corner, then back to start, then to the other diagonal corner, alternating directions. The drill builds agility, lateral speed, and cardio for athletic conditioning.

en: Set up four cones in a square pattern about 5 yards apart.
Stand at one cone (the starting cone).
Brace your core and stay light on your feet.
Sprint diagonally across the square to the opposite cone.
Touch the cone with your hand and turn around.
Sprint diagonally back to the starting cone.
Sprint laterally to the adjacent cone.
Continue running the X pattern at high speed.
Builds agility and change-of-direction speed
Strong cardio drill
Athletic conditioning
Develops footwork
Useful for sports training
Time-efficient drill
